## 9 Limitations

(1) The topology-only ablation (A2) shows a 0% \to 100% gradient but the full DAG combines multiple prompt choices not disentangled via factorial design.
(2) Stronger retrieval baselines might narrow the gap.
(3) All experiments use CDISCPilot01 (ADSL/ADAE); generalization to other studies or datasets is untested.
(4) Claude’s 100% vs. GPT-4.1’s 59% may partly reflect differential training data exposure.
(5) DAG requires 15 sequential LLM calls (662s vs. 65s for Keyword-RAG).
(6) With 1–3 runs per configuration, confidence intervals remain wide (74.5%, 95% CI: 67.5–80.5%).
(7) The 15-node DAG was manually designed ( \sim 40 hours); automated generation is future work.
Additional limitations are in Appendix E.

## 10 Conclusion

We presented GxP-Agent, a multi-agent system encoding regulatory process ordering as DAG topology for clinical trial programming.
On CDISC-Bench, GxP-Agent achieves 100% structural match on ADSL with Claude (1 Opus + 3 Sonnet runs, 0% variance)—a task where all single-shot approaches score 0% and the best retrieval-augmented baseline achieves 59.2%.
The core insight is that clinical trial programming is a compliance task: the correct decomposition and ordering of derivation steps can be determined from domain specifications a priori and encoded as graph topology, reducing the LLM’s role to generating correct R code for narrow, well-scoped subtasks.
We release CDISC-Bench and anonymized code as supplementary material to enable further research; full code and data will be released upon publication.
